{{Short description|Concepts in commutative algebra}}
In [[commutative algebra]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''going up''' and '''going down''' are terms which refer to certain properties of [[total order#Chains|chain]]s of [[prime ideal]]s in [[integral extension]]s.

The phrase '''going up''' refers to the case when a chain can be extended by "upward [[subset|inclusion]]", while '''going down''' refers to the case when a chain can be extended by "downward inclusion".

The major results are the '''Cohen–Seidenberg theorems''', which were [[mathematical proof|proved]] by [[Irvin Cohen|Irvin S. Cohen]] and [[Abraham Seidenberg]]. These are known as the '''going-up''' and '''going-down theorems'''.

== Going up and going down ==
Let ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' be an [[ring extension|extension of commutative rings]].

The going-up and going-down theorems give sufficient conditions for a chain of prime ideals in ''B'', each member of which lies over members of a longer chain of prime ideals in ''A'', to be able to be extended to the length of the chain of prime ideals in ''A''.

===Lying over and incomparability===

First, we fix some terminology. If <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> are [[prime ideal]]s of ''A'' and ''B'', respectively, such that

:<math>\mathfrak{q} \cap A = \mathfrak{p}</math>

(note that <math>\mathfrak{q} \cap A</math> is automatically a prime ideal of ''A'') then we say that <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> ''lies under'' <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> and that <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> ''lies over'' <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>. In general, a ring extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' of [[commutative ring]]s is said to satisfy the '''lying over property''' if every prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> of ''A'' lies under some prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> of&nbsp;''B''.

The extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' is said to satisfy the '''incomparability property''' if whenever <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{q}'</math> are distinct primes of ''B'' lying over a prime <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> in ''A'', then <math>\mathfrak{q}</math>&nbsp;⊈&nbsp;<math>\mathfrak{q}'</math>  and <math>\mathfrak{q}'</math>&nbsp;⊈&nbsp;<math>\mathfrak{q}</math>.

=== Going-up ===

The ring extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' is said to satisfy the '''going-up property''' if whenever

:<math>\mathfrak{p}_1 \subseteq \mathfrak{p}_2 \subseteq \!\!\;\cdots\cdots\cdots\!\!\, \subseteq \mathfrak{p}_n</math>

is a chain of prime ideals of ''A'' and

:<math>\mathfrak{q}_1 \subseteq \mathfrak{q}_2 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \mathfrak{q}_m</math>

is a chain of prime ideals of ''B'' with ''m'' < ''n'' and such that <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> lies over <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> for 1&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''m'', then the latter chain can be extended to a chain

:<math>\mathfrak{q}_1 \subseteq \mathfrak{q}_2 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \mathfrak{q}_m \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \mathfrak{q}_n</math>

such that <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> lies over <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> for each 1&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''.

In {{harv|Kaplansky|1970}} it is shown that if an extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' satisfies the going-up property, then it also satisfies the lying-over property.

=== Going-down ===

The ring extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' is said to satisfy the '''going-down property''' if whenever

:<math>\mathfrak{p}_1 \supseteq \mathfrak{p}_2 \supseteq \!\!\;\cdots\cdots\cdots\!\!\, \supseteq \mathfrak{p}_n</math>

is a chain of prime ideals of ''A'' and

:<math>\mathfrak{q}_1 \supseteq \mathfrak{q}_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathfrak{q}_m</math>

is a chain of prime ideals of ''B'' with ''m'' < ''n'' and such that <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> lies over <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> for 1&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''m'', then the latter chain can be extended to a chain

:<math>\mathfrak{q}_1 \supseteq \mathfrak{q}_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathfrak{q}_m \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathfrak{q}_n</math>

such that <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> lies over <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> for each 1&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''.

There is a generalization of the ring extension case with ring morphisms. Let ''f'' : ''A''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''B'' be a (unital) [[ring homomorphism]] so that ''B'' is a ring extension of ''f''(''A''). Then ''f'' is said to satisfy the '''going-up property''' if the going-up property holds for ''f''(''A'') in&nbsp;''B''.

Similarly, if ''B'' is a ring extension of ''f''(''A''), then ''f'' is said to satisfy the '''going-down property''' if the going-down property holds for ''f''(''A'') in ''B''.

In the case of ordinary ring extensions such as ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'', the [[inclusion map]] is the pertinent map.

==Going-up and going-down theorems==

The usual statements of going-up and going-down theorems refer to a ring extension ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'':
#(Going up) If ''B'' is an [[integral extension]] of ''A'', then the extension satisfies the going-up property (and hence the lying over property), and the incomparability property.
#(Going down) If ''B'' is an integral extension of ''A'', and ''B'' is a domain, and ''A'' is integrally closed in its field of fractions, then the extension (in addition to going-up, lying-over and incomparability) satisfies the going-down property.

There is another sufficient condition for the going-down property:
* If ''A'' ⊆ ''B'' is a [[flat extension]] of commutative rings, then the going-down property holds.<ref>This follows from a much more general lemma in Bruns-Herzog, Lemma A.9 on page 415.</ref>

''Proof'':<ref>Matsumura, page 33, (5.D), Theorem 4</ref> Let ''p''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''p''<sub>2</sub> be prime ideals of ''A'' and let ''q''<sub>2</sub> be a prime ideal of ''B'' such that ''q''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;∩&nbsp;''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''p''<sub>2</sub>. We wish to prove that there is a prime ideal ''q''<sub>1</sub> of ''B'' contained in ''q''<sub>2</sub> such that ''q''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;∩&nbsp;''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''p''<sub>1</sub>. Since ''A''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B'' is a flat extension of rings, it follows that ''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub> is a flat extension of rings. In fact, ''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub> is a faithfully flat extension of rings since the inclusion map ''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>&nbsp;→&nbsp;''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub> is a local homomorphism. Therefore, the induced map on spectra Spec(''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub>)&nbsp;→&nbsp;Spec(''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>) is [[surjective function|surjective]] and there exists a prime ideal of ''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub> that contracts to the prime ideal ''p''<sub>1</sub>''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub> of ''A''<sub>''p''<sub>2</sub></sub>. The contraction of this prime ideal of ''B''<sub>''q''<sub>2</sub></sub> to ''B'' is a prime ideal ''q''<sub>1</sub> of ''B'' contained in ''q''<sub>2</sub> that contracts to ''p''<sub>1</sub>. The proof is complete.&nbsp;'''Q.E.D.'''
